$comment: The power to change someone else's duties — to create them, alter them, or end them. Power of attorney is one. A judge's power to convict is one. An officer's power to give an order that puts a subordinate under a duty is one. Prefixed because 'power' alone is energy over time, and the enterprise means both. Exercising a power is not doing a thing you were free to do; it is making a new obligation exist. The judge's word constitutes the conviction — it is not behaviour that happens to correlate with guilt. This is why a power written as though it were a liberty has been mis-written: liberties are about what you may do, powers are about what you may make true of others. Authority, in the end, is a collection of these.

name.$comment: What the power is called, as it is said: 'installing an officer'.

under.$comment: The authority that confers it. You do not hold a power by being able to do the thing; you hold it because something says you may. Being able to sign someone else's name is not power of attorney.

alters.$comment: The duty this power creates, changes, or ends. Names an obligation and not a work: a power whose 'alters' names a thing you do, rather than a thing you make true of someone, is a liberty wearing a power's name.

over.$comment: Whose duties it may change. They are correspondingly liable — not a bad thing to be: being liable to an offer is the condition of being able to accept one. A power over nobody changes nothing.

delegated-from.$comment: The power this one was granted out of, where it was granted. Delegating is itself an exercise of power: the principal changes the agent's position by handing over some of their own. Absent on an original power — one that came from no other party inside the enterprise.

$comment-absences: No discharged-when: a power is exercised, not discharged. It makes an obligation; it is not one. No holder or bearer: the office's deontic profile is where the holder enters, and an office is largely a bundle of these.
